rows: Employers must prevent danger from electrical systems and electrical work.
Electrical installations and equipment should be suitable for their intended use.
Electrical equipment should be maintained so it remains safe.
Work on or near live electrical conductors should be avoided unless justified and controlled.
Isolation should be secure and verified before work begins where practicable.
People carrying out electrical work need appropriate competence, information and supervision.
Portable and fixed electrical equipment should be selected for the environment and foreseeable conditions.
Defects, damage and electrical incidents should trigger prompt removal from use, investigation and corrective action.
A PAT label or recent inspection does not prove that a particular electrical task or installation is safe.
Conclusions require circuit, voltage, condition, isolation, environment, protection, competence and actual-use evidence.
Employers must assess risks from occupational noise where exposure may harm hearing.
Noise exposure should be eliminated or reduced at source where reasonably practicable.
Quieter processes, equipment and work methods should be considered before relying on hearing protection.
Exposure action values and limits inform the level of control required.
Hearing protection zones and suitable protectors may be needed for residual risk.
Workers need information and training about noise hazards and protective measures.
Health surveillance is required where workers remain at risk of noise-induced hearing damage.
Noise controls should be maintained and reviewed when equipment, processes or exposure patterns change.
A spot sound-level reading or issued ear defenders do not establish a worker's daily noise exposure.
Conclusions require task duration, noise level, frequency content, controls, protector fit, maintenance and health-surveillance evidence.
Regular exposure to hand-arm vibration can cause hand-arm vibration syndrome and carpal tunnel syndrome.
Employers should assess vibration exposure from powered hand tools and work processes.
Exposure should be eliminated or reduced through equipment and process selection.
Tool condition, consumables and maintenance can materially affect vibration exposure.
Trigger time should be estimated from actual work rather than shift length alone.
Work organisation and task rotation can reduce exposure when they genuinely reduce trigger time.
Workers need information about symptoms and early reporting.
Health surveillance is required where workers remain exposed at a level presenting risk.
A tool vibration rating or shift duration alone does not establish personal exposure.
Conclusions require measured or representative vibration, trigger time, grip, tool condition, task, controls and surveillance evidence.
Whole-body vibration can affect people who drive or ride mobile machinery and vehicles.
Employers should assess exposure where vibration may create a health risk.
Poor road or ground condition, speed and vehicle suspension can increase exposure.
Suitable vehicle selection and maintenance can reduce vibration.
Seats should be adjusted and maintained for the driver and operating conditions.
Route planning and speed control can reduce shocks and vibration.
Work schedules should manage exposure duration and recovery.
Controls should be reviewed when vehicles, routes or operating conditions change.
A seat specification or vehicle type does not determine an individual's whole-body vibration exposure.
Conclusions require vehicle, route, speed, seat, posture, duration, shocks, maintenance and actual operating evidence.
